keywords.definition_en: A strong, often irresistible urge to act, especially against one's conscious wishes
keywords.definition_pl: Silna, często nieodparta potrzeba działania, zazwyczaj wbrew własnej woli
keywords.example_en: His constant checking of social media felt like a compulsion he couldn't control.
keywords.example_pl: Jego ciągłe sprawdzanie mediów społecznościowych było jak przymus, którego nie mógł kontrolować.

commonCollocations.example: Widespread compulsion has become a major concern in modern society.
The committee aims to address the compulsion through new legislation.
Steps must be taken to prevent compulsion before it escalates.

contexts.example: Understanding compulsion in education is crucial for policy makers.
The rise of compulsion has sparked debate across the country.

usagePatterns.example: The initiative was launched to reduce compulsion in affected communities.
New measures have been introduced to combat compulsion effectively.

synonyms.nuance: Use for persistent, intrusive thoughts that dominate the mind. WRONG for describing external pressure or legal requirements — don't say 'tax obsession' when you mean compulsion to pay taxes.
Use when force or threats compel action. WRONG for describing internal drives — don't say 'I felt coercion to check my phone' when you mean a personal habit.
Use for internal motivation, often positive. WRONG for describing addictive or harmful behaviors — don't say 'his drive to gamble' in formal contexts.
Use for pathological, uncontrollable urges. WRONG for casual contexts — don't say 'I have an obsessive need for coffee' unless clinically diagnosed.

falseFriends.polishMeaning: rarely used; compulsion in Polish often sounds like 'compulsory' meaning
falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may confuse compulsion (internal urge) with compulsory (mandatory/required) — these are different concepts

commonMistakes.mistake: I have a compulsion to go to school
commonMistakes.correction: I am compelled to go to school / School is compulsory
commonMistakes.reason: L1 interference — Polish 'kompulsywny' suggests addiction, while English 'compulsion' can mean any irresistible urge; learners confuse internal compulsion with external obligation

learnerNotes.usageTip: Remember: compulsion comes from inside (you can't stop yourself), compulsory comes from outside (rules require it).

keywords.example_en: The new strategy focuses on maximising the positives in teamwork.
keywords.example_pl: Nowa strategia skupia się na maksymalizowaniu pozytywów pracy zespołowej.

synonyms.nuance: Use when highlighting advantages to persuade customers. WRONG for personal development contexts — don't say 'I'm accentuating the benefits of my marriage'.
Use for risk-return calculations and portfolio management. WRONG for everyday emotional contexts — don't say 'I'm optimising the upside of my vacation'.
Use for casual, optimistic reframing. WRONG for formal business reports — don't say 'We're focusing on the bright side of our quarterly losses'.
Use for organisational or personal development frameworks. WRONG for describing emotional coping — don't say 'I'm leveraging my strengths to deal with grief'.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may use 'maximise' too literally, forgetting it needs an object — 'maximising' alone is incomplete

commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization — Polish countable/uncountable noun rules differ; 'positive' as noun is usually plural in this phrase

learnerNotes.usageTip: This phrase is common in British business English — use it when discussing how to handle change or challenges optimistically.

keywords.example_pl: Dobrzy liderzy potrafią skutecznie minimalizować negatywy w trudnych sytuacjach.

synonyms.nuance: Use for formal reduction of risks or adverse effects. WRONG for casual emotional contexts — don't say 'I'm mitigating the drawbacks of my breakup'.
Use when deliberately making problems seem smaller. WRONG for genuine problem-solving — don't say 'We're downplaying the disadvantages' if you mean actually solving them.
Use for hedging strategies and loss prevention. WRONG for interpersonal contexts — don't say 'I'm limiting the downside of our friendship'.
Use when responding to already-occurred problems. WRONG for proactive prevention — don't say 'We're doing damage control' before any damage has happened.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may confuse this with 'minimalist' lifestyle concepts, not realizing it means reducing harm in strategic contexts

commonMistakes.reason: L1 interference — Polish speakers translate 'strony negatywne' literally instead of using the natural collocation

learnerNotes.usageTip: Often paired with 'maximising the positives' — together they describe an optimistic, strategic approach to any situation.

keywords.definition_en: To improve the quality or value of life by adding meaningful or beneficial experiences
keywords.definition_pl: Poprawiać jakość lub wartość życia poprzez dodanie wartościowych doświadczeń
keywords.example_en: Learning a new language can truly enrich one's life.
keywords.example_pl: Nauka nowego języka może naprawdę wzbogacić życie.

usagePatterns.example: This approach helps students enrich one's life complex concepts more easily.

synonyms.nuance: Use for profound, almost existential improvement. WRONG for casual everyday improvements — don't say 'Netflix enhances my existence'.

synonyms.synonym: to add value to one's life
synonyms.nuance: Use for measurable, intentional improvements. WRONG for emotional/spiritual contexts — don't say 'Meditation adds value to my life' (sounds too corporate).
Use specifically for gaining new perspectives through travel or learning. WRONG for material improvements — don't say 'A new car broadened my horizons'.
Use for holistic, intentional lifestyle development. WRONG for quick fixes — don't say 'This app cultivates a fuller life'.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may associate this only with money/wealth, not realizing English 'enrich' is commonly used for non-material life improvement

commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization — Polish learners sometimes treat 'rich' as a verb; 'enrich' is the correct verb form

learnerNotes.usageTip: This phrase elevates your vocabulary — use it for hobbies, travel, relationships, or learning that makes life more meaningful, not for basic necessities.

keywords.definition_pl: Bardzo wyraźna różnica pomiędzy dwiema rzeczami
keywords.example_en: The peaceful village was in stark contrast to the noisy city.
keywords.example_pl: Spokojna wieś była w wyraźnym kontraście do hałaśliwego miasta.

synonyms.nuance: Use for noticeable, attention-grabbing differences. WRONG for extreme opposites — 'striking' is weaker than 'stark'.
Use for clear categorical boundaries. WRONG for visual comparisons — don't say 'a sharp distinction in colours'.
Use for problematic or unjust differences. WRONG for neutral comparisons — don't say 'a glaring disparity between vanilla and chocolate'.
Use when contrasting elements create discomfort or surprise. WRONG for natural, harmonious differences — don't say 'a jarring juxtaposition' if you mean pleasant variety.

falseFriends.polishMeaning: not a Polish word; learners may confuse with 'sztywny' (stiff)
falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers unfamiliar with 'stark' may avoid it or confuse it with 'stiff/rigid' rather than understanding it means 'harsh, blunt, complete'

commonMistakes.reason: Vocabulary limitation — Polish learners often default to 'strong' when 'stark' (more precise, emphatic) is the natural collocation

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Stark' means harsh, blunt, or complete — use it when differences are extreme and impossible to ignore, not just noticeable.

keywords.definition_en: Trying to influence or control others in a clever, often unfair or dishonest way
keywords.definition_pl: Próba wpływania lub kontrolowania innych w sprytny, często nieuczciwy sposób
keywords.example_en: The advertisement used manipulative tactics to convince people to buy the product.
keywords.example_pl: Reklama używała manipulacyjnych taktyk, aby przekonać ludzi do zakupu produktu.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes manipulative as a key issue.
There is growing concern about manipulative.
The article explores the role of manipulative in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating manipulative in modern society.
You can see manipulative in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on manipulative in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to manipulative.

synonyms.nuance: Use when someone intentionally lies to achieve goals. WRONG for subtle emotional influence — deceit requires false statements, manipulation doesn't.
Use for dominating behavior in relationships. WRONG for one-time deceptive acts — controlling implies ongoing pattern.
Use for calculated, secretive planning. WRONG for spontaneous manipulation — scheming requires premeditation.
Use when taking unfair advantage of vulnerability. WRONG for peer-to-peer manipulation — exploitation implies power imbalance.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may use 'manipulative' more neutrally, not realizing it's strongly negative in English; Polish 'manipulować' can sound technical/skill-based

commonMistakes.correction: He is a very manipulative person
commonMistakes.reason: Article omission — Polish doesn't use articles, so learners frequently drop them before noun phrases

learnerNotes.usageTip: In English, 'manipulative' is always negative — don't use it to describe someone who's simply persuasive or skilled at handling objects.

keywords.definition_en: Relating to laws or the making of laws
keywords.definition_pl: Dotyczący praw lub tworzenia praw
keywords.example_en: The legislative changes will affect all citizens.
keywords.example_pl: Zmiany ustawodawcze wpłyną na wszystkich obywateli.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly legislative by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly legislative as the deadline approached.

contexts.example: What sounds legislative in theory may fail in practice.
The reform must be legislative for families, not only for experts.

usagePatterns.example: The plan may become legislative if funding is approved.
The target seemed legislative at first, but the team stayed cautious.

synonyms.nuance: Use specifically for laws created by statute. WRONG for describing the branch of government — 'statutory branch' is incorrect.
Use for systems centered on parliament. WRONG for US contexts — the US has Congress, not Parliament.
Use for plain English explanations. WRONG for formal legal documents — too informal for contracts or court filings.
Use for rule-making by executive agencies. WRONG for elected bodies — regulatory bodies are typically appointed, not elected.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may confuse legislative (making laws) with legal (related to law in general) — these are distinct concepts

commonMistakes.reason: Word form confusion — 'legislative' is an adjective; the noun form is 'legislature' for the body

learnerNotes.usageTip: Remember: legislative = adjective (describes things related to making laws), legislature = noun (the actual law-making body).

keywords.definition_en: The act of supervising or monitoring something to make sure it is done correctly or safely. Sometimes it can also mean an accidental mistake, but in this context it means supervision.
keywords.definition_pl: Działanie polegające na nadzorowaniu lub monitorowaniu czegoś, aby upewnić się, że jest wykonywane poprawnie lub bezpiecznie. Czasami może też oznaczać przypadkowy błąd, ale w tym kontekście oznacza nadzór.
keywords.example_en: The project was completed under the oversight of experienced managers.
keywords.example_pl: Projekt został ukończony pod nadzorem doświadczonych menedżerów.

commonCollocations.example: The agency was created to provide regulatory oversight of the sector.
Critics demanded stronger government oversight after the scandal.
The report blamed the failure on a lack of oversight.

contexts.example: Better oversight in banking could reduce systemic risk.
Parliament is responsible for oversight of public spending.

usagePatterns.example: An independent board should provide oversight of the project.
The reform aims to strengthen oversight without slowing innovation.

synonyms.nuance: Use for direct monitoring of employees or projects. WRONG for accidental errors — supervision doesn't mean 'mistake'.
Use for critical, detailed examination. WRONG for routine monitoring — scrutiny implies suspicion or high standards.
Use for covert or systematic observation. WRONG for normal management — surveillance implies watching without consent.
Use when oversight means a mistake (unintentional failure). WRONG for the monitoring meaning — 'government omission' doesn't mean supervision.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may not realize 'oversight' has two opposite meanings: careful supervision AND an accidental mistake

commonMistakes.mistake: It was an oversight from the manager
commonMistakes.correction: It was an oversight by the manager / There was a lack of oversight from the manager
commonMistakes.reason: Preposition confusion — Polish case system doesn't map directly; learners mix up 'from' and 'by' with oversight

learnerNotes.usageTip: Context is crucial — 'oversight' can mean careful monitoring (good) OR a mistake from not noticing (bad). Check which meaning fits.

keywords.definition_en: To grow, develop, or succeed in a strong and healthy way. It can describe people, businesses, ideas, or even plants.
keywords.definition_pl: Rozwijać się, rozwijać lub odnosić sukcesy w silny i zdrowy sposób. Może opisywać ludzi, firmy, pomysły, a nawet rośliny.
keywords.example_en: Small businesses can flourish in supportive communities.

synonyms.nuance: Use for successful growth in challenging conditions. WRONG for artistic/creative success — thriving sounds biological or economic.
Use specifically for financial or material success. WRONG for personal happiness without wealth — don't say 'she prospered emotionally'.
Use for gradual, beautiful development of potential. WRONG for rapid business growth — too gentle/romantic for corporate contexts.
Use for rapid, visible growth. WRONG for established success — burgeoning implies beginning to grow, not already flourishing.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may misspell or mispronounce due to similarity with 'flour' — these are homophones but different words

commonMistakes.reason: Spelling/pronunciation interference — the 'sh' sound is spelled differently; Polish speakers may add an extra 'i'

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'flourish' for thriving in a holistic sense — health, happiness, success combined — not just financial growth.

keywords.definition_en: make sth as large or effective as possible
keywords.definition_pl: sprawiać, że coś jest tak duże lub efektywne, jak to możliwe
keywords.example_en: We should maximise our study time to prepare for the exam.
keywords.example_pl: Powinniśmy zmaksymalizować czas nauki, aby przygotować się do egzaminu.

You can see maximise in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on maximise in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: Use for finding the best balance of multiple factors. WRONG when you mean purely increasing quantity — optimization may involve trade-offs.
Use for taking advantage of opportunities. WRONG for resource management — capitalizing requires an opportunity, not just resources.
Use for making something larger by adding to it. WRONG for efficiency contexts — augmenting increases size, not necessarily efficiency.
Use for increasing signal, effect, or reach. WRONG for simple addition — amplifying multiplies effect, not just adds.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may overuse this word in contexts where English prefers specific verbs like 'optimize' or 'increase'

commonMistakes.mistake: We need to maximise our time
commonMistakes.correction: We need to make the most of our time / use our time efficiently
commonMistakes.reason: Collocation error — 'maximise time' is unnatural; English prefers idiomatic expressions for time management

learnerNotes.usageTip: British spelling uses 's' (maximise), American uses 'z' (maximize) — be consistent within your document.

keywords.definition_en: reduce something to the smallest possible amount
keywords.definition_pl: redukować coś do najmniejszej możliwej ilości
keywords.example_en: She tried to minimise distractions while working from home.
keywords.example_pl: Starała się minimalizować rozpraszacze podczas pracy z domu.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes minimise as a key issue.
There is growing concern about minimise.
The article explores the role of minimise in modern life.

You can see minimise in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on minimise in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to minimise.

synonyms.nuance: Use for general decrease in quantity. WRONG when zero is the goal — reducing implies some remains, minimizing aims for least possible.
Use for making negative effects less severe. WRONG for cost reduction — mitigation is for harm, not expenses.
Use for cutting back or restricting activities. WRONG for natural processes — curtailing implies deliberate limitation.
Use specifically for reducing workforce or operations. WRONG for reducing risk or waste — downsizing means making smaller, not safer.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may use 'minimise' when 'reduce' or 'decrease' would sound more natural in everyday English

commonMistakes.correction: eliminate the risks / reduce the risks to a minimum
commonMistakes.reason: Logical contradiction — minimizing means making as small as possible, not necessarily zero; Polish logic may treat 'minimalny' as 'none'

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'minimise' for strategic reduction to the lowest practical level, not complete elimination — that's 'eliminate' or 'eradicate'.

Use for improving quality or value of existing things. WRONG for adding new elements — enhancing improves what's there, doesn't add new substance.
Use for adding decorative details. WRONG for factual contexts — embellishing implies possible exaggeration or ornamentation.
Use for providing with quality, ability, or funding. WRONG for casual improvement — endowing is formal and substantial.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may limit 'enrich' to financial or agricultural contexts, missing its broader use for experiences and education

learnerNotes.usageTip: Enrich implies adding something valuable that creates depth — use it for education, culture, soil, uranium, and life experiences.

keywords.definition_en: a clear difference between two things
keywords.definition_pl: wyraźna różnica między dwiema rzeczami

synonyms.nuance: Use for dramatic differences in data or situations. WRONG: 'The colors have sharp contrast' — use for visual arts, not metaphorical differences.
More conversational than stark contrast. WRONG in technical reports where 'stark' conveys severity better.
Emphasizes uncomfortable or unsettling contrast. WRONG for neutral statistical comparisons.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may think 'stark' just means 'strong' and use it for positive emphasis, but it carries negative/severe connotations.

commonMistakes.reason: L1 interference — 'silny kontrast' is natural in Polish but 'strong contrast' sounds weak/childish in English.
Spelling confusion — Polish speakers may mix up similar-looking words.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'stark' when you want to emphasize how shocking or severe the difference is — it's stronger than just 'big difference'.

keywords.definition_en: reduce the severity or seriousness of sth
keywords.definition_pl: zmniejszać nasilenie lub powagę czegoś
keywords.example_en: The company is taking steps to mitigate the environmental damage.
keywords.example_pl: Firma podejmuje kroki w celu złagodzenia szkód środowiskowych.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes mitigate as a key issue.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating mitigate in modern society.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on mitigate in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: Use for pain, symptoms, suffering. WRONG for financial or legal risks — use 'mitigate' instead.

Formal term for making symptoms bearable without curing. WRONG in business contexts — sounds overly clinical.
Simpler, more accessible. WRONG in formal legal/technical documents where precision matters.

falseFriends.confusion: Completely different meaning — Polish speakers may avoid 'mitigate' thinking it relates to myths.

commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization — confusing with 'guard against'. 'Mitigate' is transitive: 'mitigate risks' not 'mitigate against risks'.
False word creation — Polish speakers may invent this thinking it means 'make minimal'.

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Mitigate' always needs an object — you mitigate something (risk, damage, impact), never just 'mitigate' alone.

keywords.definition_en: doing sth within reasonable limits; not too much

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Toggle' originally meant a fastener on clothing; in tech, it means quickly switching between exactly two states — perfect for describing multitasking on computers.

commonMistakes.reason: Usage pattern — a bottleneck is a point/thing, not a 'that' clause.

Describes things/actions without value. WRONG for people — 'pointless person' is odd.

Activity done for enjoyment. WRONG as adjective — it's a noun.
Emphasizes lack of serious competition. WRONG for general fun activities.

falseFriends.confusion: Similar spelling — Polish speakers may confuse 'recreational' with 'recruitment' activities.

commonMistakes.reason: False word creation — Polish 'rekreacyjny' pattern doesn't directly translate.
Redundancy — 'recreational' already implies 'for fun/enjoyment'.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'recreational' for activities done for enjoyment rather than work — but be careful with 'recreational drugs' as it specifically means illegal substance use, not just 'fun medicine'.

keywords.example_pl: Próbował obejść system bezpieczeństwa, używając fałszywego dowodu.

Avoid addressing directly. WRONG for physical obstacles — implies evasion, not physical navigation.
Escape from, often with negative connotation. WRONG for legitimate workarounds — implies dishonesty.
Avoid dealing with. WRONG in formal technical documentation — too informal.

falseFriends.confusion: Similar beginning — Polish speakers may confuse spelling or pronunciation.

commonMistakes.reason: Redundancy — 'circumvent' already means 'go around', don't add 'around'.
Word confusion — 'circulate' means to move around in a circle or distribute.

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Circumvent' often carries a slightly negative tone — it suggests finding a clever way around rules or obstacles, sometimes implying rule-breaking.

Gradual weakening of foundations or authority. WRONG for physical landscape changes.
General worsening of state. WRONG when emphasizing gradual wearing-away process specifically.
Physical gradual removal. WRONG for abstract concepts in formal writing.

commonMistakes.reason: Article usage — abstract uncountable nouns like 'trust' don't take 'the' in general statements.
Spelling — remember the 'e' before the 's' in third person singular.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Think of water slowly wearing away rock over years — use 'erodes' for gradual, destructive change to things that should be solid (trust, values, land, rights).

keywords.definition_en: Movies, games, or books that gain a passionate fan following over time, even if not popular at first.
keywords.definition_pl: filmy, gry lub książki, które z czasem zyskują pasjonującą grupę fanów, nawet jeśli początkowo nie były popularne
keywords.example_en: That horror film flopped at release but later became a cult classic.
keywords.example_pl: Ten horror początkowo okazał się klapą, ale później stał się kultowym klasykiem.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes cult classics as a key issue.

synonyms.nuance: Use for movies/music with niche fanbases that never achieved mainstream success. WRONG: Don't use for mainstream blockbusters like Titanic or commercially successful franchises.
Use for films that became popular slowly over time despite initial commercial failure. WRONG: Don't use for films that were immediately successful or had huge marketing budgets.
Interchangeable with cult classics but slightly less formal. WRONG: Don't use for universally beloved mainstream works like The Beatles or Star Wars (original trilogy was mainstream).

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may think 'cult' only has negative religious connotations and avoid the phrase, not realizing it also means 'passionate niche following'.

commonMistakes.reason: L1 word order interference; Polish adjectives often precede nouns differently, and 'classic' vs 'classical' confusion (classical = ancient Greek/Roman, classic = exemplary/of high quality).

learnerNotes.usageTip: Remember that 'cult' here is positive—it means dedicated fans, not something dangerous or religious.

keywords.definition_en: The obligation to accept responsibility for actions and decisions.
keywords.definition_pl: obowiązek przyjęcia odpowiedzialności za działania i decyzje
keywords.example_en: The manager showed accountability by admitting his mistake.
keywords.example_pl: Kierownik wykazał się odpowiedzialnością, przyznając się do błędu.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes accountability as a key issue.

You can see accountability in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on accountability in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to accountability.

synonyms.nuance: Use when emphasizing the obligation to explain decisions to stakeholders or the public. WRONG: Don't use for personal friendships or casual contexts—sounds bureaucratic and cold.
Broader term for duty and ownership of tasks. WRONG: Don't use when you specifically mean 'consequences for failure'—responsibility lacks the enforcement/oversight aspect.
Use when referring to legal obligation or financial exposure for damages. WRONG: Don't use for workplace performance management—sounds like you're discussing lawsuits, not job duties.

falseFriends.confusion: The 'account' in accountability sounds like Polish 'konto', making Polish speakers think it relates to banking or bookkeeping rather than responsibility.

commonMistakes.mistake: He has accountability for the project
commonMistakes.correction: He is accountable for the project / He has accountability
commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization from 'have responsibility'; 'accountability' as a noun doesn't take 'for' after 'have' in this structure.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'accountable to someone' (who you report to) and 'accountable for something' (what you're responsible for)—never mix these prepositions.

keywords.definition_en: Being open and clear about actions, decisions, or information.
keywords.definition_pl: bycie otwartym i jasnym w kwestii działań, decyzji lub informacji

Use when emphasizing understandable, jargon-free information. WRONG: Don't use when you mean 'full disclosure of all data'—clarity can hide information while making what's shown clear.
Use for ability to track processes or data flow in real-time. WRONG: Don't use for ethical disclosure or governance contexts—sounds mechanical, not principled.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'transparentny' often means 'obvious/blatant' (negative), while English 'transparency' in business is always positive, meaning honest disclosure.

commonMistakes.correction: The company operates with full transparency / The company is fully transparent
commonMistakes.reason: Polish grammar interference—Polish uses 'mieć' (have) where English uses 'be' or action verbs.

learnerNotes.usageTip: In business English, 'transparency' is always positive—unlike Polish where 'transparentny' can mean 'obviously dishonest'.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may think 'undermine' is only literal (mining tunnels), not realizing it's almost always used figuratively for authority, confidence, or systems.

commonMistakes.correction: He undermines my work / He causes me to do bad work
commonMistakes.reason: Confusion with 'persuade' structure; 'undermine' takes a direct object (what is damaged), not an infinitive construction.

commonMistakes.mistake: He undermines me to do bad work
commonMistakes.correction: He undermines my work / He causes me to do bad work
commonMistakes.reason: Confusion with 'persuade' structure; 'undermine' takes a direct object (what is damaged), not an infinitive construction.

keywords.definition_en: to make an action or process easier

Use for speeding up processes or making them happen faster. WRONG: Don't use for collaborative discussion or creative work—expedite implies rushing, not quality interaction.
Use for making difficult situations less burdensome or painful. WRONG: Don't use for formal business processes—sounds too casual and emotional.

commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization from 'provide you with'; 'facilitate' takes the process/task as object, not the person.

keywords.definition_en: to give out something to several people or spread over an area
keywords.definition_pl: rozdzielać coś kilku osobom lub rozprzestrzeniać na danym obszarze
keywords.example_en: The organization distributes food to families in need.

Use for spreading information, documents, or viruses through a population. WRONG: Don't use for one-time delivery of goods—circulation implies ongoing movement and repetition.
Use for giving out specific quantities, especially medication or from machines. WRONG: Don't use for large-scale logistics or bulk distribution—dispense implies controlled, measured portions.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'dystrybucja' is almost exclusively business/supply chain, while English 'distribute' is used much more broadly—handing out papers, sharing tasks, etc.

commonMistakes.mistake: The teacher distributed the students into groups
commonMistakes.correction: The teacher divided the students into groups / distributed the worksheets to the students
commonMistakes.reason: False friend with Polish 'rozdzielić'; 'distribute' requires things being given out, not people being organized.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Distribute needs a physical or digital thing being handed out—use 'divide' or 'assign' for organizing people.

keywords.definition_en: to distribute resources or duties for a particular purpose
keywords.definition_pl: przydzielać zasoby lub obowiązki do określonego celu
keywords.example_en: The manager decided to allocate more funds to marketing.
keywords.example_pl: Menedżer zdecydował o przydzieleniu większych środków na marketing.

Use for giving tasks, people, or resources to specific purposes or owners. WRONG: Don't use for budget planning without specific recipients—assignment implies designated owners, not just amounts.

falseFriends.confusion: The 'locate' in allocate makes Polish speakers think it means finding where something is, not distributing resources.

commonMistakes.mistake: We allocated the team to the project
commonMistakes.correction: We assigned the team to the project / allocated budget to the project
commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization; 'allocate' is for resources (money, time, materials), 'assign' is for people and tasks.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Allocate = resources (money, time, materials); Assign = people and tasks—don't mix them.

keywords.definition_en: to combine several things into a single more effective unit; to make something stronger
keywords.definition_pl: łączyć kilka rzeczy w jedną bardziej efektywną całość; umacniać coś
keywords.example_en: The company plans to consolidate its operations in Europe.
keywords.example_pl: Firma planuje konsolidację swoich operacji w Europie.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes consolidate as a key issue.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating consolidate in modern society.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on consolidate in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: Use for combining separate companies or entities into one. WRONG: Don't use for organizing data or strengthening market position—merger implies legal combination, not just operational efficiency.

Use for bringing dispersed functions or data under single control. WRONG: Don't use for debt refinancing or financial consolidation—centralization is about control location, not financial restructuring.
Use for making a position, advantage, or structure more secure and powerful. WRONG: Don't use for combining multiple items into fewer—strengthening doesn't imply reduction in number.

falseFriends.polishMeaning: consolidation (financial: combining debts; EU: political integration)
falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'konsolidacja' is heavily financial/EU political, while English 'consolidate' is used broadly—combining files, strengthening gains, centralizing operations.

commonMistakes.mistake: We consolidated the meeting to Tuesday
commonMistakes.correction: We consolidated the meetings into one on Tuesday / rescheduled the meeting for Tuesday
commonMistakes.reason: Confusion with 'concentrate' or Polish 'skupić'; 'consolidate' requires multiple items being combined, not just moving one item.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Consolidate always implies 'combining multiple things into fewer/one'—you need at least two items to consolidate.

keywords.definition_en: having the right to do or obtain something; satisfying the appropriate conditions
keywords.definition_pl: mający prawo do zrobienia lub uzyskania czegoś; spełniający odpowiednie warunki
keywords.example_en: Only eligible candidates will be considered for the scholarship.
keywords.example_pl: Tylko kwalifikujący się kandydaci zostaną rozpatrzeni w sprawie stypendium.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes eligible as a key issue.
There is growing concern about eligible.
The article explores the role of eligible in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating eligible in modern society.
You can see eligible in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on eligible in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to eligible.

synonyms.nuance: Use for having the necessary skills, experience, or credentials. WRONG: Don't use for meeting age, residency, or other non-skill requirements—qualification is about competence, not criteria.
Use for having a legal right or claim to something. WRONG: Don't use for competitive selection processes—entitlement is about rights, not meeting selection criteria.
Use for being allowed or authorized to do something. WRONG: Don't use for benefit programs or scholarships—permission is about authorization, not meeting requirements for access.

falseFriends.confusion: Similar pronunciation makes Polish speakers confuse 'eligible' (meeting requirements) with 'elite' (exclusive/best), opposite meanings.

commonMistakes.mistake: I am eligible to get the visa
commonMistakes.correction: I am eligible for the visa
commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization from 'able to get'; 'eligible' takes 'for' (the thing), not 'to' + verb.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Eligible + FOR (noun), not eligible + TO (verb)—say 'eligible for the discount' not 'eligible to get the discount'.

keywords.definition_en: fair and impartial; dealing fairly and equally with all concerned
keywords.definition_pl: sprawiedliwy i bezstronny; traktujący wszystkich uczestników uczciwie i równo
keywords.example_en: We need to find an equitable solution to this dispute.
keywords.example_pl: Musimy znaleźć sprawiedliwe rozwiązanie tego sporu.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly equitable by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly equitable as the deadline approached.
It became politically equitable after public support grew.

contexts.example: What sounds equitable in theory may fail in practice.
The reform must be equitable for families, not only for experts.

usagePatterns.example: The plan may become equitable if funding is approved.
The target seemed equitable at first, but the team stayed cautious.

synonyms.nuance: Use for everyday situations of justice and impartiality. WRONG: Don't use for legal documents or formal policy—sounds too casual and vague.
Use for absence of bias in decision-making or reporting. WRONG: Don't use for resource distribution or outcome fairness—impartial is about process neutrality, not result fairness.
Use for distribution or response matching the scale of input or provocation. WRONG: Don't use for moral fairness discussions—proportionate is mathematical/measured, not ethical.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers with finance background may confuse 'equitable' (fair) with 'equity' (shares/ownership capital)—completely different concepts.

commonMistakes.mistake: The equitable was reached in court
commonMistakes.correction: Equity was reached / An equitable settlement was reached

synonyms.nuance: Use on official forms. WRONG when describing temporary holiday visits or short stays.
Use in casual discussion. WRONG when referring to homeless shelter accommodation or hospital stays.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish uses 'u' (at someone's place), but English requires 'with' for cohabitation; 'live by parents' means near them, not together.

commonMistakes.reason: Calque from Polish 'u rodziców' (at parents'); learners use 'by' thinking it means 'at/near.'
Polish 'być na utrzymaniu rodziców' (be financially supported by parents) leads to confusion between 'with' (location) and 'on' (financial support).

learnerNotes.usageTip: Always use 'with' for sharing a home, not 'by' or 'on.'

keywords.definition_en: the age range during which women are biologically capable of conceiving and giving birth, typically 15-49
keywords.definition_pl: przedział wiekowy, w którym kobiety są biologicznie zdolne do poczęcia i urodzenia dziecka, zazwyczaj 15-49 lat
keywords.example_en: Many women are delaying having children until their late childbearing years.
keywords.example_pl: Wiele kobiet odkłada posiadanie dzieci na późne lata rozrodcze.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes childbearing years as a key issue.
There is growing concern about childbearing years.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating childbearing years in modern society.
You can see childbearing years in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on childbearing years in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to childbearing years.

synonyms.nuance: Use in clinical or medical contexts. WRONG when discussing career planning or education timelines.
Use for crops or livestock. WRONG when applied to humans in formal medical contexts.

falseFriends.confusion: Some Polish speakers confuse 'bearing' with 'bierny' (passive) or unrelated words, not realizing it means 'carrying/giving birth.'

commonMistakes.reason: Polish 'lata rodzenia dzieci' uses the plural 'dzieci', so learners pluralize 'child.'
Word-for-word translation from Polish 'lata rodzenia dzieci'; English compounds the noun and gerund into one word.

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Childbearing' is one word (or hyphenated), and 'child' stays singular.

keywords.definition_en: relating to political groups or ideologies that hold extreme conservative or nationalist views
keywords.definition_pl: odnoszący się do grup politycznych lub ideologii głoszących skrajnie konserwatywne lub nacjonalistyczne poglądy
keywords.example_en: The far-right lawmaker used a fire extinguisher on the menorah lighting ceremony.
keywords.example_pl: Poseł skrajnej prawicy użył gaśnicy podczas ceremonii zapalania menorah.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly far-right by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly far-right as the deadline approached.
It became politically far-right after public support grew.

The reform must be far-right for families, not only for experts.

usagePatterns.example: The plan may become far-right if funding is approved.
The target seemed far-right at first, but the team stayed cautious.

synonyms.nuance: Use when describing strict traditionalism. WRONG when describing nationalist movements that are economically left-wing.
Use in news reporting. WRONG in academic sociology where 'radical right' is the preferred technical term.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may write 'far right' without the hyphen when it functions as an adjective before a noun, which is incorrect in English.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish treats political groups as countable plural nouns, but in English 'far-right' is uncountable as a group.
Redundancy caused by combining Polish 'skrajna prawica' with English 'wing.'

learnerNotes.usageTip: Hyphenate 'far-right' before a noun (e.g., 'far-right party'), but no hyphen after the noun (e.g., 'the party is far right').

keywords.definition_en: a person who makes or enacts laws, especially a member of a legislative body
keywords.definition_pl: osoba tworząca lub wprowadzająca w życie prawa, szczególnie członek organu ustawodawczego
keywords.example_en: The Polish lawmaker was suspended after the incident in parliament.
keywords.example_pl: Polski poseł został zawieszony po incydencie w parlamencie.

commonCollocations.example: A working lawmaker often needs flexible childcare.
Single lawmakers may face extra financial pressure.
She became a lawmaker in her early thirties.

contexts.example: The article shows what life as a lawmaker at home can look like.
Local services should support every lawmaker in the community.

usagePatterns.example: Good policy should support a lawmaker, not punish them.
Teachers should talk to a lawmaker before making assumptions.

synonyms.nuance: Use for elected officials who create statutes. WRONG when referring to judges or lawyers who interpret law but do not create it.
Use exclusively for members of the US Congress. WRONG when referring to members of parliamentary systems outside the United States.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'prawnik' is a broad term for any legal professional, so learners often confuse 'lawmaker' (politician who writes laws) with 'lawyer' (person who practices law).

commonMistakes.reason: Polish 'prawnik' covers both lawmakers and lawyers, so learners use 'lawyer' for politicians who create legislation.
Learners sometimes create a compound from Polish 'twórca prawa' but choose the wrong components.

learnerNotes.usageTip: A lawmaker makes laws in parliament; a lawyer practices law in court.

keywords.definition_en: a portable device that discharges a jet of water, foam, gas, or other material to extinguish a fire
keywords.definition_pl: przenośne urządzenie wypuszczające strumień wody, piany, gazu lub innego materiału do gaszenia pożaru
keywords.example_en: He grabbed a fire extinguisher and sprayed it at the candles.
keywords.example_pl: Chwycił gaśnicę i psiknął nią na świece.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes fire extinguisher as a key issue.
There is growing concern about fire extinguisher.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on fire extinguisher in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: Use for the chemical agent itself. WRONG when referring to the portable red handheld device.
Use as casual shorthand. WRONG in official safety inspection reports where the full term 'fire extinguisher' is mandatory.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'gaśnica' comes from 'gasić' (to extinguish), but learners may confuse 'extinguisher' with 'extinction' (Polish 'wymarcie').

commonMistakes.reason: Polish speakers often add 'machine' to devices because Polish uses '-arka' or '-nica' suffixes that imply machinery.
Calque from Polish 'gaśnica pożarowa'; learners reverse the noun order thinking it needs 'of.'

learnerNotes.usageTip: Never add 'machine' — just say 'fire extinguisher.'

keywords.definition_en: a seven- or nine-branched candelabrum used in Jewish religious celebrations, especially Hanukkah
keywords.definition_pl: siedmio- lub dziewięcioramienny świecznik używany w żydowskich obrzędach religijnych, szczególnie podczas Chanuki
keywords.example_en: The annual menorah lighting ceremony was interrupted by the protest.
keywords.example_pl: Coroczna ceremonia zapalania menorah została przerwana przez protest.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes menorah as a key issue.
There is growing concern about menorah.
The article explores the role of menorah in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating menorah in modern society.
You can see menorah in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on menorah in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: Use for any branched candlestick. WRONG when referring specifically to the Jewish ritual object, which requires 'menorah.'
Use for the ancient Temple menorah. WRONG when talking about the Hanukkah nine-branched version, which is technically a hanukkiah.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish borrows the word as 'menora' without the final 'h', so learners drop the 'h' in English.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish spelling/pronunciation interference; Polish lacks this exact sound pattern, so learners drop the 'e' or change vowels.
Polish phonology tends to drop final 'h' sounds or replace them with vowels, leading to Polishized spelling.

learnerNotes.usageTip: The final 'h' is pronounced — say 'meh-NO-rah,' not 'meh-NO-ra.'

keywords.definition_en: to extinguish something, especially a flame; to put an end to something
keywords.definition_pl: zgasić coś, szczególnie płomień; położyć kres czemuś
keywords.example_en: The MP snuffed out the Hanukkah candles with a fire extinguisher.
keywords.example_pl: Poseł zgasił świece chanukowe gaśnicą.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes snuff out as a key issue.
There is growing concern about snuff out.
The article explores the role of snuff out in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating snuff out in modern society.
You can see snuff out in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on snuff out in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to snuff out.

synonyms.nuance: Use for neutral, technical descriptions of fires. WRONG when describing the suppression of a rebellion or hope, where 'snuff out' carries a violent, conclusive nuance.
Use for suppressing rebellions or legal decisions. WRONG when talking about candles or literal fires.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may associate 'snuff' with 'snuć' due to similar spelling, but they are completely unrelated.

commonMistakes.reason: Dropping the particle 'out'; in Polish 'zdmuchnąć' is a perfective verb that does not need a particle, so learners omit 'out.'
Redundancy — 'snuff out' already means to completely extinguish, so adding 'completely' is unnecessary.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Always include 'out' — 'snuff' alone refers to powdered tobacco.

keywords.definition_en: to extinguish a fire or light with water or another liquid; to soak thoroughly
keywords.definition_pl: zgasić ogień lub światło wodą lub inną cieczą; dokładnie nasączyć
keywords.example_en: He doused the flames before they could spread.
keywords.example_pl: Zgasił płomienie, zanim mogły się rozprzestrzenić.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes douse as a key issue.
There is growing concern about douse.
The article explores the role of douse in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating douse in modern society.
You can see douse in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on douse in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to douse.

synonyms.nuance: Use when someone gets soaked by rain. WRONG in firefighting contexts where 'douse' implies deliberate suppression of flames.
Use for fabrics absorbing liquid. WRONG when putting out fires; it implies absorption rather than throwing liquid on.

falseFriends.confusion: The spelling similarity leads Polish speakers to associate 'douse' with choking, but it means to pour liquid on something, especially to extinguish a fire.

commonMistakes.reason: Spelling confusion — 'dowse' means to search for water with a divining rod, while 'douse' means to extinguish with liquid.
Polish 'oblać benzyną' means to cover with gasoline to burn something, but English 'douse' means to put OUT a fire with liquid — the opposite meaning.

learnerNotes.usageTip: 'Douse' means to put OUT a fire with water or liquid, not to set it on fire.

keywords.definition_en: temporarily prevented from holding office, participating, or attending as a form of punishment
keywords.definition_pl: tymczasowo pozbawiony możliwości sprawowania urzędu, uczestnictwa lub uczęszczania jako forma kary
keywords.example_en: The lawmaker was suspended from parliament for his actions.

Use for applications or job offers. WRONG in parliamentary procedure where 'suspended' is the required technical term.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'zawieszony' means both suspended (temporarily stopped) and hanged (by a noose), leading to confusion between 'suspended' and 'hanged.'

commonMistakes.reason: Direct translation of Polish 'zawieszony' without recognizing that 'hanged' refers to execution by hanging.
Overgeneralization — Polish 'zawieszony' is used for both temporary procedural suspension and physical hanging, but English distinguishes them.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'suspended' for temporary stops or exclusions, and 'hanged' only for execution by rope.

keywords.definition_en: the highest legislature, consisting of elected representatives who make laws for a country
keywords.definition_pl: najwyższy organ ustawodawczy, składający się z wybranych przedstawicieli tworzących prawa dla kraju
keywords.example_en: The incident took place inside the Polish parliament building.
keywords.example_pl: Incydent miał miejsce w budynku polskiego parlamentu.

synonyms.nuance: Use for the law-making body as an institution. WRONG when referring to the physical building or chamber.
Use for one house within a bicameral system. WRONG when referring to the entire parliament including both houses.

falseFriends.confusion: Identical meaning, but Polish spelling lacks the 'i' (parlament vs parliament), and Polish grammar treats it as plural.

commonMistakes.reason: In Polish, institutions like 'parlament' often take plural verbs, but in English 'parliament' takes a singular verb.
Polish spelling interference — Polish writes it as 'parlament' without the 'i', and learners sometimes keep Polish spelling.

learnerNotes.usageTip: In English, 'parliament' is singular and spelled with an 'i' after the 'l'.

keywords.definition_en: a Jewish festival lasting eight days, celebrating the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem
keywords.definition_pl: żydowski święto trwające osiem dni, obchodzone na cześć ponownego poświęcenia Świątyni w Jerozolimie
keywords.example_en: Hanukkah is also known as the Festival of Lights.
keywords.example_pl: Chanuka jest znana również jako Święto Świateł.

synonyms.nuance: Alternative transliteration from Hebrew, equally correct. Use when writing for Jewish audiences or academic religious contexts. WRONG: Using in general English contexts where 'Hanukkah' is the standard spelling.
Descriptive term used when explaining the holiday to non-Jewish audiences. WRONG: Using in formal Jewish religious contexts where 'Hanukkah' is expected.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish speakers often drop double letters due to Polish phonology where doubled consonants are rare and not distinctive.
Overcorrection - Polish 'ch' represents /x/ sound, but Hebrew 'ח' is often transliterated as just 'h' in English.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use 'Hanukkah' (with double 'k') as the standard spelling in general English; 'Chanukah' is acceptable but less common.

keywords.definition_en: to carry out a systematic or formal inquiry to discover and examine the facts of something
keywords.definition_pl: przeprowadzić systematyczne lub formalne dochodzenie w celu odkrycia i zbadania faktów dotyczących czegoś
keywords.example_en: Prosecutors are investigating the lawmaker for his actions.
keywords.example_pl: Prokuratorzy prowadzą dochodzenie w sprawie posła za jego działania.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes investigate as a key issue.
There is growing concern about investigate.
The article explores the role of investigate in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating investigate in modern society.
You can see investigate in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on investigate in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to investigate.

synonyms.nuance: Implies deep, often aggressive inquiry into wrongdoing. Use for serious scandals or corruption. WRONG: Using for routine research or casual curiosity ('I probed the menu').
Systematic, methodical analysis. Use for scientific or scholarly contexts. WRONG: Using for criminal matters where 'investigate' or 'probe' is expected.
Informal, preliminary inquiry. Use when promising to check something. WRONG: Using in formal reports or legal documents.
Official financial examination. Use specifically for reviewing accounts. WRONG: Using for general criminal investigations.

falseFriends.confusion: Both share Latin root 'investire' but diverged in meaning. Polish speakers may say 'I will investigate money' meaning 'I will invest money'.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish requires a preposition ('zbadać coś' - no preposition, but 'zainwestować w coś' - with preposition), causing confusion.
Polish 'zrobić' translates broadly; 'make' with 'investigation' is non-idiomatic in English.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Remember: you 'investigate' something directly (no preposition), but you 'invest in' something.

title: Meat, Metrics & Modern Poland

keywords.definition_en: a person who supports or argues in favor of an idea, plan, or theory. It's similar in meaning to 'supporter' or 'advocate,' but sounds a bit more formal.
keywords.definition_pl: osoba popierająca lub argumentująca na rzecz idei, planu lub teorii. Podobne znaczenie do 'zwolennik' lub 'adwokat', ale brzmi nieco bardziej formalnie.
keywords.example_en: Many proponents of renewable energy believe it's the key to fighting climate change.
keywords.example_pl: Wielu zwolenników energii odnawialnej uważa, że to klucz do walki ze zmianami klimatu.

commonCollocations.example: A working proponent often needs flexible childcare.
Single proponents may face extra financial pressure.
She became a proponent in her early thirties.

contexts.example: The article shows what life as a proponent at home can look like.
Local services should support every proponent in the community.

usagePatterns.example: Good policy should support a proponent, not punish them.
Teachers should talk to a proponent before making assumptions.

synonyms.nuance: Active, vocal supporter often arguing publicly. Use for passionate defenders of causes. WRONG: Using for neutral supporters or when implying mere agreement without action.
Broader, less formal term. Use for general backing without implying active campaigning. WRONG: Using when emphasizing the intellectual or argumentative aspect of support.
Enthusiastic leader promoting a cause. Use for organizational or change management contexts. WRONG: Using in neutral academic analysis where it sounds too promotional.
Person who explains or interprets a theory. Use for intellectual traditions or schools of thought. WRONG: Using for political supporters where 'proponent' or 'advocate' fits better.

falseFriends.confusion: Similar spelling but completely different meaning. Polish speakers may confuse 'proponent' with someone making a proposal.

commonMistakes.reason: Prefix confusion - 'pro-' (for) vs 'op-' (against). Polish 'przeciwnik' (opponent) and 'zwolennik' (proponent) have no shared root.

commonMistakes.correction: a proponent of something / in favor of doing something
commonMistakes.reason: Polish grammar allows 'zwolennik robienia czegoś' (genitive of verb), but English prefers noun phrase or restructuring.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Proponent = someone FOR something; opponent = someone AGAINST something. The 'pro-' prefix means 'for'.

keywords.definition_en: to increase the selling price of a product, usually to make a profit. The markup is the difference between the cost of something and its selling price.
keywords.definition_pl: zwiększyć cenę sprzedaży produktu, zazwyczaj w celu osiągnięcia zysku. Marża to różnica między kosztem czegoś a jego ceną sprzedaży.
keywords.example_en: The store marked up all winter coats before the holiday season.
keywords.example_pl: Sklep podniósł ceny wszystkich zimowych płaszczy przed sezonem świątecznym.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes mark up as a key issue.
There is growing concern about mark up.
The article explores the role of mark up in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating mark up in modern society.
You can see mark up in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on mark up in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to mark up.

synonyms.nuance: Neutral term for raising price. Use when no specific business mechanism is implied. WRONG: Using when the business practice of adding margin is the key point.
Sharp, often sudden increase. Use for dramatic price rises. WRONG: Using for standard business markup practices.
Technical term for profit calculation. Use in financial analysis. WRONG: Using in consumer-facing contexts.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may associate 'mark up' with branding due to 'marka' meaning brand.

commonMistakes.correction: mark up (a price) / mark up the document
commonMistakes.reason: Phrasal verb has two meanings: raising prices (business) OR annotating/editing (publishing). Context determines meaning.

commonMistakes.correction: apply a markup / mark up the price
commonMistakes.reason: Polish noun-based thinking ('zrobić marżę') leads to unidiomatic English.

learnerNotes.usageTip: As a verb: 'mark up' (two words). As a noun: 'markup' (one word). Example: 'We markup products' is wrong; say 'We mark up products' or 'We apply a markup'.

keywords.definition_en: to increase the price of something, especially goods before selling them to customers
keywords.definition_pl: podwyższać cenę czegoś, szczególnie towarów przed sprzedażą klientom
keywords.example_en: Some restaurants mark up wine prices by more than 200%.
keywords.example_pl: Niektóre restauracje zawyżają ceny wina o ponad 200%.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes mark up as a key issue.
There is growing concern about mark up.
The article explores the role of mark up in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating mark up in modern society.
You can see mark up in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on mark up in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to mark up.

synonyms.nuance: Add explanatory notes or comments. Use for documents, texts, or images. WRONG: Using for price increases in business contexts.
Make corrections or improvements. Use for drafts and manuscripts. WRONG: Using when only comments are added without changes.
Add metadata labels. Use for HTML or data classification. WRONG: Using for handwritten document review.

commonMistakes.reason: As a verb, it must be two words. 'Markup' is the noun form.

commonMistakes.mistake: mark up the price (when meaning annotate)
commonMistakes.correction: mark up the document / annotate the document
commonMistakes.reason: Same phrasal verb, different meaning. Polish learners often don't recognize the ambiguity.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Context is everything: 'mark up prices' = raise prices; 'mark up a document' = add comments/corrections. Check the object!

keywords.definition_en: a regular payment from the government to people who need financial help, such as those who are unemployed, disabled, or elderly
keywords.definition_pl: regularna płatność od rządu dla osób potrzebujących pomocy finansowej, takich jak bezrobotni, niepełnosprawni lub osoby starsze
keywords.example_en: Families earning below the income threshold are eligible for social assistance.
keywords.example_pl: Rodziny zarabiające poniżej progu dochodowego kwalifikują się do pomocy finansowej.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes social grant as a key issue.
There is growing concern about social grant.
The article explores the role of social grant in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating social grant in modern society.
You can see social grant in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on social grant in practical contexts.

synonyms.nuance: General term for government assistance. Use in American contexts. WRONG: Using in South African contexts where 'social grant' is the official term.
Broad term for state support. Use in British English contexts. WRONG: Using when specific grant programs are discussed.
Regular fixed payment, often for specific purposes. Use for student or research funding. WRONG: Using for means-tested poverty relief.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'grant' typically means research funding, not social welfare payments.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish lacks the /gr/ vs /græ/ distinction; Polish speakers may substitute Polish vowel sounds.

commonMistakes.mistake: a social grant from the government
commonMistakes.reason: Redundancy - grants are by definition from government/institutions. Polish 'zasiłek od rządu' encourages this.

learnerNotes.usageTip: In South Africa, 'social grant' is the official term; in other countries, use 'welfare payment' or 'benefit' instead.

keywords.definition_en: the quality of being fair and impartial; the value of the shares issued by a company; or the value of a property after deducting charges against it
keywords.definition_pl: jakość bycia sprawiedliwym i bezstronnym; wartość akcji wydanych przez firmę; lub wartość nieruchomości po odliczeniu obciążeń
keywords.example_en: Equity means providing resources based on individual needs to achieve fair outcomes.
keywords.example_pl: Sprawiedliwość oznacza zapewnianie zasobów w oparciu o indywidualne potrzeby w celu osiągnięcia sprawiedliwych rezultatów.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes equity as a key issue.
There is growing concern about equity.
The article explores the role of equity in modern life.

contexts.example: Experts are still debating equity in modern society.
You can see equity in everyday life, not only in theory.

usagePatterns.example: The final chapter focuses on equity in practical contexts.
Communities need better ways to respond to equity.

synonyms.nuance: Moral concept of just treatment. Use in DEI (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) contexts. WRONG: Using in financial contexts where 'equity' means ownership stake.
Net assets of a company. Use in balance sheet analysis. WRONG: Using in social contexts where it sounds like corporate jargon.
Ownership interest in a company. Use for startup investment discussions. WRONG: Using when referring to home ownership value.
Legal right to property. Use for home equity discussions. WRONG: Using for stock market investments.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish business English uses 'ekwity' only for financial meaning; learners may not know the social justice meaning.

commonMistakes.reason: Polish 'równość' covers both concepts. English distinguishes: equality = same treatment, equity = fair treatment accounting for circumstances.

commonMistakes.mistake: the equity of the company is good
commonMistakes.correction: the company has strong equity / the company's equity position is strong
commonMistakes.reason: Polish syntax allows adjective description directly; English prefers noun phrases.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Equity has opposite meanings: in finance = ownership/value; in social contexts = fairness. Always check the context!

keywords.definition_en: specific income levels that determine whether someone qualifies for a certain tax rate, benefit, or financial assistance
keywords.definition_pl: określone poziomy dochodów, które determinują, czy ktoś kwalifikuje się do określonej stawki podatkowej, świadczenia lub pomocy finansowej
keywords.example_en: Many middle-class workers are just above the income threshold for state support.
keywords.example_pl: Wielu pracowników klasy średniej zarabia tuż powyżej progu dochodowego uprawniającego do pomocy państwa.

commonCollocations.example: The report describes income threshold as a key issue.
There is growing concern about income threshold.

Without prejudice. WRONG: Personal preferences → implies complete neutrality, not just openness.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish 'otwarty' means physically open or frank/direct, not necessarily 'willing to consider new ideas' like 'open-minded'.

commonMistakes.correction: He is open-minded / He has an open mind

commonMistakes.reason: Preposition error: Polish 'dla' (for) interferes; English uses 'to' or 'about'

synonyms.nuance: Use for places far from population centers. WRONG: 'remote schedule' — say 'irregular schedule' instead.
Use for private, hidden locations like beaches or villas. WRONG: 'secluded opinion' — opinions cannot be secluded.
Use for places cut off from transport or communication. WRONG: 'isolated task' — say 'standalone task' instead.
Use for places physically impossible to reach. WRONG: 'inaccessible person' — say 'unapproachable person' instead.

falseFriends.polishMeaning: get out of the way / move aside
falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers confuse 'out-of-the-way' (remote) with the literal translation 'z drogi' which means to move aside or stop obstructing.

commonMistakes.mistake: The shop is out of way
commonMistakes.correction: The shop is out of the way

Use for negotiations or conflicts lasting longer than expected. WRONG: 'protracted sandwich' — use for processes, not objects.
Use for stories, scenes, or speeches that feel too long. WRONG: 'drawn-out building' — use for temporal experiences, not structures.

commonMistakes.mistake: It spends a lot of time
commonMistakes.correction: It takes a lot of time / It is time-consuming
commonMistakes.reason: L1 interference from Polish 'pożerać czas' (devours time) or direct translation of 'spędzać czas' (spend time) which refers to people, not tasks.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Remember that tasks 'take' time or are 'time-consuming'; they never 'spend' time.

keywords.example_en: The meeting was tedious and seemed to last forever.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly tedious by the review panel.

synonyms.nuance: Use for repetitive tasks or sounds without variation. WRONG: 'monotonous flavour' — flavours vary, use 'bland'.
Use for people or situations that exhaust your patience. WRONG: 'tiresome landscape' — landscapes don't actively tire you, use 'boring'.
Use for bleak, depressing atmospheres or weather. WRONG: 'dreary maths problem' — maths isn't atmospheric, use 'tedious'.
Use for work so boring it feels like it shuts down your brain. WRONG: 'mind-numbing tragedy' — tragedies are emotionally painful, not boring.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish learners sometimes confuse 'tedious' with 'tremendous' because of the similar -ous ending and syllable count, saying something is 'tedious' when they mean 'amazing'.

commonMistakes.reason: Overgeneralization: 'tedious' describes tasks or processes that are long and boring, not social events or entertainment.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Reserve 'tedious' for work, tasks, or processes that are long and boring, not for parties or films.

keywords.definition_en: likely to become successful or popular soon
keywords.definition_pl: prawdopodobnie wkrótce odnoszący sukces lub zyskujący popularność

keywords.example_pl: Jest obiecującą projektantką w branży modowej.

Use for stars or teams climbing rankings or fame. WRONG: 'rising library' — libraries don't climb ranks, use 'growing'.
Use for young people beginning to show talent. WRONG: 'budding CEO with 30 years experience' — contradictory, use 'established'.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers confuse 'up-and-coming' (promising future success) with 'nadchodzący' which simply means 'coming soon' or 'approaching' in time.

commonMistakes.reason: Wrong hyphenation and confusion with 'upcoming' (nadchodzący). 'Up-and-coming' always needs all three words and hyphens when used as an adjective.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Do not confuse 'up-and-coming' (promising success) with 'upcoming' (happening soon).

Use for expressing opinions firmly and respectfully. WRONG: 'assertive wallpaper' — only for people or communication styles.
Use for someone who remains calm and in control of emotions. WRONG: 'self-possessed bicycle' — only for people.

falseFriends.polishMeaning: self-assured / confident (but often implies cockiness in Polish)
falseFriends.confusion: In Polish, 'pewny siebie' can sound negative (cocky/arrogant), whereas 'self-assured' in English is almost always positive or neutral.

commonMistakes.reason: Direct calque from Polish 'pewny siebie' translated word-for-word. English does not use 'self-sure'.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Avoid the Polish calque 'self-sure'; always use 'self-assured' or 'confident'.

synonyms.nuance: Use for direct, honest communication without evasion. WRONG: 'forthright wallpaper pattern' — only for people or statements.
Use for brutally direct speech that may offend. WRONG: 'blunt weather' — weather cannot be intentionally direct, use 'harsh'.
Use for honest, unguarded remarks or interviews. WRONG: 'candid building' — buildings cannot hide opinions, use 'plain'.
Use for people who openly express strong opinions. WRONG: 'vocal table' — inanimate objects cannot speak, use 'noisy' for sound.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may confuse 'outspoken' with 'wyszczekany' (rude, talking back), but 'outspoken' means frank and direct, not necessarily disrespectful.

commonMistakes.reason: Omission of the prefix 'out-' because Polish 'wymowny' (eloquent) or 'gadatliwy' (talkative) do not contain an equivalent prefix.

learnerNotes.usageTip: You must include the 'out-' prefix; 'spoken' alone means articulate or eloquent, not frank or direct.

keywords.definition_en: ordinary; not special or unusual
keywords.definition_pl: zwykły; nie wyjątkowy ani niezwykły
keywords.example_en: It was just a run-of-the-mill presentation, nothing exciting.
keywords.example_pl: To była po prostu przeciętna prezentacja, nic ekscytującego.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly run-of-the-mill by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly run-of-the-mill as the deadline approached.
It became politically run-of-the-mill after public support grew.

The reform must be run-of-the-mill for families, not only for experts.

usagePatterns.example: The plan may become run-of-the-mill if funding is approved.
The target seemed run-of-the-mill at first, but the team stayed cautious.

synonyms.nuance: Use for work that is below average or uninspired. WRONG: 'mediocre emergency surgery' — implies unacceptable quality for life-critical tasks.
Use for common items with no special features. WRONG: 'ordinary genius' — contradictory, use 'unassuming'.
Use for things so average they leave no impression. WRONG: 'unremarkable heroism' — heroic acts are by definition notable.
Use for products meeting normal specifications. WRONG: 'standard masterpiece' — contradictory, masterpieces exceed standards.

falseFriends.confusion: Polish speakers may take the idiom literally because of the word 'mill' (młyn), thinking it relates to flour production rather than ordinariness.

commonMistakes.mistake: It's a run of mill product
commonMistakes.reason: Missing hyphens and the definite article 'the'. Polish has no articles and learners often omit them in fixed expressions.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Always include 'the' and use hyphens when this phrase modifies a noun: a run-of-the-mill product.

keywords.definition_en: sensible and practical
keywords.definition_pl: rozsądny i praktyczny
keywords.example_en: Despite her fame, she's very down-to-earth.
keywords.example_pl: Pomimo sławy jest bardzo twardo stąpająca po ziemi.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly down-to-earth by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly down-to-earth as the deadline approached.
It became politically down-to-earth after public support grew.

contexts.example: What sounds down-to-earth in theory may fail in practice.
The reform must be down-to-earth for families, not only for experts.

usagePatterns.example: The plan may become down-to-earth if funding is approved.
The target seemed down-to-earth at first, but the team stayed cautious.

synonyms.nuance: Use for practical, results-oriented decision-making. WRONG: 'pragmatic rainbow' — natural phenomena cannot be practical.
Use for budgets, expectations, or portrayals grounded in truth. WRONG: 'realistic stone' — stones are literally real, not realistic.
Use for emotionally stable, sensible people. WRONG: 'grounded airplane' — means physically fixed to the ground, not sensible.
Use for practical, reasonable choices or rules. WRONG: 'sensible earthquake' — natural disasters cannot be reasonable.

falseFriends.confusion: In Polish, 'przyziemny' can mean vulgar or coarse (earthy), whereas in English 'down-to-earth' is always positive, meaning practical and realistic.

commonMistakes.mistake: He is down to the earth
commonMistakes.correction: He is down to earth / He is a down-to-earth person
commonMistakes.reason: Adding an unnecessary article 'the' due to L1 interference from Polish 'przyziemny' or confusion with the idiom 'come down to earth'.

learnerNotes.usageTip: Use hyphens only when the phrase comes before a noun (a down-to-earth guy); after a verb, no hyphens are needed (He is down to earth).

keywords.definition_en: relaxed and not easily worried or upset
keywords.definition_pl: wyluzowany i niełatwo się przejmujący lub złoszczący
keywords.example_en: He's so easy-going that nothing seems to bother him.
keywords.example_pl: Jest tak wyluzowany, że nic go nie rusza.

commonCollocations.example: The proposal was considered highly easy-going by the review panel.
The situation looked increasingly easy-going as the deadline approached.
It became politically easy-going after public support grew.
